name: Piz Buin

lead: Piz Buin is a European sun care brand used for holiday and outdoor sun protection and a steadier, less burnt tan. Less sunburn and sun damage means more even, healthier-looking skin.

It traces to Franz Greiter's 1946 Gletscher Crème and is named after an Alpine mountain. Sunscreen filters as a class are well studied; for the brand itself, published use is limited to old 1980s mouse experiments.

paras: People apply it to exposed skin before sun exposure and reapply through the day, choosing the SPF to suit their skin type. It is used on holidays and for outdoor sport, and some pair it with after-sun care.
Sunscreen lowers but does not eliminate sunburn and UV damage, and it works only as long as it is applied generously and reapplied. No human studies of the brand were found.

angle.text: Piz Buin is a European sun care brand, descended from a 1946 glacier cream, used for outdoor sun protection and a steadier tan. UV filters in the cream cut burning and sun damage, which keeps skin tone more even and healthy-looking.

lead: Piz Buin is a European sun care brand of sunscreens and after-sun products. People use it to get a tan or time outdoors while limiting sunburn, which keeps skin looking even and helps avoid the redness, peeling and uneven tone that follow burning.[1][2]

According to Wikipedia, Austrian chemist Franz Greiter introduced a product called Gletscher Crème (Glacier Cream) in 1946 that became the basis for the Piz Buin company, named after the Alpine mountain where Greiter reportedly got sunburned. The article estimates that the early cream had an SPF of about 2.[1][2]

Greiter is also credited with the sun protection factor. In 1974 he adapted earlier calculations by Friedrich Ellinger and Rudolf Schulze and introduced SPF as a measure of UVB protection, which became a global standard.[2] Published scientific use of the brand itself is limited to 1980s animal experiments in which a Piz Buin product served as a test sunscreen.[3][4]
infobox: 3,312 m summit on the Austria-Switzerland border; first ascent 14 July 1865 [5]

paras: Greiter's 1946 glacier cream was the basis for the brand. Wikipedia credits the name to the mountain where he allegedly suffered sunburn.[1][2] Piz Buin is also a peak in the Silvretta Alps on the Austria-Switzerland border.
In 1974 Greiter introduced the sun protection factor, adapting earlier calculations by Ellinger and Schulze.[2]

Wikipedia's sunscreen article places Greiter's cream in a longer lineage: ancient Greeks used olive oil and zinc oxide paste is thousands of years old; Australian chemist H.A. Milton Blake made an early tannic-acid sunscreen in 1932; German researchers at IG Farben tested filters in the 1930s under the Delial line; and Benjamin Green's 1944 'Red Vet Pet' for US forces was followed by Coppertone and Bain de Soleil in the early 1950s.[1] After Greiter introduced SPF in 1974, water-resistant sunscreens followed in 1977.[1]

Grokipedia describes the mountain behind the name as the highest summit in the Austrian state of Vorarlberg, a double peak in the Silvretta Alps at 3,312 metres, first climbed on 14 July 1865 by Joseph Anton Specht and Johann Jakob Weilenmann; it is AI-generated text and is cited only for the mountain's description.[5]

Sunscreen is used to stay out in the sun with less burning, and so with less of the redness, peeling and uneven tone that follow a burn. Wikipedia notes that SPF measures UVB protection, the radiation that mainly causes sunburn, while UVA penetrates deeper, causes little reddening but contributes to DNA damage, skin ageing and melanoma risk, so 'broad-spectrum' products are designed to cover both.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports that a 2013 Australian study of about 900 participants found daily broad-spectrum sunscreen use for 4.5 years led to smoother, more resilient skin, an ageing study rather than a skin-cancer trial.[1] Piz Buin lines are sold both as protection and for people who want to tan gradually; Wikipedia does not describe the brand's current product range or filters, and no human study of the brand itself was found.

SPF measures the fraction of sunburn-producing UV rays that reach the skin; an SPF 15 product lets about one-fifteenth of that burning radiation through when applied at the testing dose of 2 mg per square centimetre.[2] It reflects UVB protection specifically, and Wikipedia notes UVA also contributes to skin damage without causing much reddening. A higher SPF does not mean longer-lasting protection, and sunscreens are typically reapplied about every two hours.[2]

Sunscreens use mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, which mainly absorb UV with some reflection and scattering, or chemical (organic) filters that absorb UV and release it as lower-energy radiation, or hybrids of the two.[1] In the United States sunscreen is regulated as an over-the-counter drug; the FDA adopted SPF in 1978 and in 2021 classified only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide as generally recognised as safe and effective.[1] In the European Union sunscreen is a cosmetic, labels are capped at SPF 50+, and a UVA protection factor of at least one-third of the SPF is required for the UVA seal.[1]

Wikipedia reports that some sunscreen ingredients can cause allergic contact dermatitis, that sunscreen can reduce vitamin D synthesis although typical use usually does not cause deficiency, and that a 2019 Valisure test found benzene in 27 percent of aerosol sunscreens tested, traced to propellant impurities rather than active ingredients and followed by voluntary recalls.[1] Hawaii banned oxybenzone and octinoxate in 2018 over concerns about coral.[1] Wikipedia notes sunscreen can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, with little evidence it prevents basal cell carcinoma.[1]

No studies found in humans. Animal studies exist: a 1984 hairless-mouse study used Piz Buin 12 Sun Protection Cream at full strength and in dilutions to compare protection against vascular injury and epidermal cell damage,[3] and a 1985 study of long-term UV exposure of mouse eyes included a group protected with a Piz Buin factor 6 lotion alongside one using a factor 5 product and an unprotected group.[4]

lore.intro: Piz Buin itself is rarely discussed in appearance forums; sunscreen use and tanning are discussed as a category.
